qs.q: A 55-year-old man presents with an acute, right-sided, non-reducing varicocele. What is the most crucial next clinical step?
o: Reassure patient as normal physiological variant.
Aspirate pampiniform plexus to relieve congestion.
Request imaging to investigate retroperitoneal tumour.
qs.e: An acute, right-sided, or non-reducing varicocele suggests an obstructing retroperitoneal or renal tumour such as renal cell carcinoma, necessitating urgent imaging. Routine varicoceles are typically left-sided and decompress when supine.
qs.s: Testicular Tumours, Hydrocele and Varicocele: MCQs

qs.q: An adolescent male is diagnosed with a varicocele associated with abnormal semen parameters and ipsilateral testicular atrophy. What are the established clinical indications for treating this varicocele?
o: Pain, infertility with abnormal semen, and testicular atrophy
Asymptomatic presentation with normal physical growth parameters
Cosmetic patient preference and uncomplicated transillumination
Acute right-sided swelling with absent inguinal cough impulse
qs.e: Indications for varicocele treatment include pain, infertility with abnormal semen, and testicular atrophy in adolescents. Asymptomatic incidental varicoceles do not routinely require intervention.
qs.s: Testicular Tumours, Hydrocele and Varicocele: MCQs

qs.q: A 62-year-old man presents with a left-sided varicocele that does not empty when he lies down, alongside macroscopic haematuria. What is the precise mechanism responsible for this physical sign?
o: Direct invasion of the pampiniform plexus by a collecting duct carcinoma
Thrombosis of the inferior vena cava extending to the common iliac vein
Tumour thrombus obstructing the left testicular vein at the renal vein
Direct compression of the left spermatic artery by retroperitoneal nodes
qs.e: An acute left varicocele that does not empty on lying down occurs when a tumour thrombus obstructs the left testicular vein at its entry into the left renal vein. This is a classic local clinical sign of renal cell carcinoma.
